dashboards.name: Memory Tier Advanced - Clusters
dashboards.description: Sizing a vSphere estate for NVMe memory tiering, from metrics the vCenter adapter already collects.

config.title: How to read this
config.editorData:
Memory tiering sizing — sample. Every tile below reads a metric the vCenter adapter already collects. No super metrics are required for this dashboard; if you import supermetric.json as well, the derived figures become available for a second screen.

This is a sizing tool, not a monitoring tool. It answers what hardware would this workload need if it were tiered. On a vSphere 8 estate there is no tiering to report, which is the point — the assessment happens before the upgrade.

Reading this on a cluster that already has tiering enabled? Then mem|host_provisioned is presented memory — installed DRAM plus the NVMe tier — not installed DRAM. Measured on a tiered lab host: 639.4 GiB presented against a 127.9 GiB DRAM tier, a 5.00× overstatement. Every tile labelled presented memory says presented for that reason. On an untiered vSphere 8 host the two are the same number.

Tiles show the latest sample, not a peak. Sizing must be done on business-cycle peaks, which need a View transformation rather than a dashboard tile. Treat these values as a shape check, not as the number on the quote.

config.title: Field reference
config.editorData:
What each figure means

Available — mem|host_provisioned, summed over the cluster's hosts. The memory the hypervisor presents. On an untiered vSphere 8 host this is installed DRAM; on a host that already has tiering it is DRAM plus the NVMe tier, which is why it is labelled presented throughout.

Allocated — mem|guest_provisioned, summed over the cluster's VMs. Memory configured to guests whether or not they ever touch it, and the figure a tiered host must present. It appears three times on the cluster table, and the comparison is the point.

Allocated (all VMs) is the raw rollup and an upper bound: powered-off VMs and templates keep reporting configured memory. · Allocated (powered on) counts only running VMs — size against this one. · Allocated (powered off) is the gap between them, measured at 20.3% of allocated on one estate. A large value is both a reclamation opportunity and a warning that anything derived from the raw figure is overstated by that much.

Consumed — mem|consumed_average. Host physical memory actually backing guest pages, plus hypervisor overhead. Always less than or equal to allocated, and usually well below it.

Active — mem|active_average. The working set: pages the guests are reading or writing. This is the number tiering turns on, because the working set is what must stay in DRAM. It is an ESXi estimate from sampling, not a measurement, and it is the reason both DRAM figures below carry margin.

Tierable of used — (consumed − active) / 2. Cold memory: backed in DRAM today but outside the working set, so a candidate for NVMe. Halved deliberately, because claiming all of it assumes the working set never moves.

It is an upper bound, and on a vSAN or NSX cluster a loose one. Consumed is a host figure and includes memory that was never granted to any guest — vSAN, NSX and hypervisor structures — none of which can be tiered. Measured on a 4-host vSAN cluster over a 30-day peak: consumed 626.4 GB against granted 508.7 GB, so 117.8 GB — 19% of consumed, and about 27% of the tierable figure — was host overhead rather than cold guest memory. Compare mem|granted_average against mem|consumed_average on the host list to size the gap on your own estate before trusting this column.

The two DRAM numbers, and why there are two

DRAM required — floor is peak active. The aggressive number: at peak, every page the guests touch fits in DRAM and everything else lives on NVMe. It is a floor, not a recommendation. No margin for growth, none for the working set shifting, and none for active being an estimate.

DRAM required — conservative is peak active × 4. The planning number: the working set with 4× headroom. The factor is a starting point and is meant to be tuned once real peaks from a full business cycle are in hand.

Both are only as good as the word "peak". A super metric cannot compute a maximum over a window — it produces one value per collection. Because both formulas are linear in active, max(k × active) equals k × max(active), so setting a widget or View to the Maximum transformation over 30 days turns either into a genuine peak-based figure. Read straight off a scoreboard tile they are the latest sample, which on a quiet Sunday sizes the purchase off a trough.

Implied DRAM share at floor tells you which supported ratio the workload could carry: 50% is 1:1, 33% is 1:2, 20% is 1:4. Below 20% the workload is colder than the platform's maximum ratio allows, so the ratio is the limit rather than the workload — worth saying out loud in front of a customer.

Sanity check, and what this screen cannot see

Active of consumed is the check on the whole exercise. Typical estates run 8–12%, nearer 15% where databases dominate. Outside roughly 5–20%, suspect the metric rather than the workload — a cluster reading 1% active is a collection problem, and it would otherwise look like the best tiering candidate you own.

vCenter cannot see large pages — this pack collects them itself. No performance counter in vCenter reports guest page size or large-page backing — every counter mentioning "page" concerns zero pages, compression, swap or page-fault latency, and the vCenter adapter exposes only three VM advanced settings, none of them the relevant ones (measured across 208 VM properties). That is why this pack ships its own collector: the MemTierAdvanced adapter reads the settings straight from vSphere and publishes them as properties on every powered-on VM and host. 2 MB pages are not a disqualifier — they are broken down under pressure — so only the 1 GB opt-in counts.

Reserved memory is visible and IS a disqualifier: a VM whose reservation equals its configured memory is pinned to DRAM and cannot be tiered however cold it looks. Both halves are columns on the VM list — Reserved (configured) against the VM's configured memory. A memory limit is shown beside it for the same reason.

Disqualifiers: what cannot be tiered, and how this pack finds it

A pinned VM cannot be tiered however cold it looks. Five disqualifiers are collected and counted as pinned:

PCI passthrough or vGPU — forces a 100% memory reservation. A GPU host full of vGPU VMs has every byte pinned and cannot be tiered at all. This is the one most likely to catch you out. · Latency sensitivity = High — forces full reservation and CPU pinning. · memoryReservationLockedToMax — reservation tracks configured memory forever. · 1 GB pages — explicit per-VM opt-in, stays pinned. · Full memory reservation — reservation equal to configured memory. This also covers Fault Tolerance, since FT VMs are fully reserved.

NUMA node affinity is collected and shown per VM but deliberately not counted as pinned: it does not stop a VM being tiered, it constrains which node's DRAM it can use. The DRAM tier is per-NUMA-node, so pinned-to-a-node VMs size against that node rather than the host. VM % remote memory does not exist in Operations at any version, so affinity is the only signal available.

The two RAM-saved figures are gross, not net of pinned memory — deliberately. They are built only from vCenter metrics, so they still compute on an estate where this pack's collector has not been configured. Pinned memory (GB) and pinned VMs sit beside them as their own columns, and tierable memory (GB) is allocated already net of pinned. To get net savings, subtract pinned memory from the saved figure yourself — or read tierable memory, which has done it for you.

The pinned columns are only meaningful once the MemTierAdvanced adapter instance is configured. Until it collects they read blank or zero, which looks identical to a clean estate. Confirm the pinned VM count on the VM list before quoting anything — a blank there means "not measured", not "none".

CPU: the other half of consolidation

Memory tiering buys consolidation — more VMs per host, because each host presents more memory. Consolidation is gated by whichever resource runs out first, so a cluster already short of CPU gains nothing from extra presented memory. Read CPU headroom % against Active of host RAM %: the smaller number is the binding constraint. Tiering pays where memory binds first.

Worst VM ready % and VMs facing ready % are the ones to act on, and they often change the answer. Ready time means vCPUs waiting for a physical core — and it is frequently caused by oversized VMs, where a VM with far more vCPUs than it uses must wait for all of them to be schedulable at once. Right-size those and CPU utilisation falls, headroom appears, and memory becomes the binding constraint. A cluster that looks CPU-bound today can be a good tiering candidate after rightsizing, which is why the Oversized by column sits on the VM list beside ready.

CPU io wait is a different bottleneck again — cores idle waiting on storage, not on each other. High io wait with low utilisation means the fix is in the storage path, and neither rightsizing nor tiering will touch it.

If a cluster shows a DRAM requirement of zero, do not believe it. Both DRAM figures are derived from active memory, so a cluster whose active metric is missing or reads zero produces a DRAM requirement of zero — which presents as "this cluster needs no DRAM" rather than as a collection failure. Check Active of consumed first: a plausible cluster sits in the 5–20% band, and anything reading near zero is a broken metric, not a cold workload.
